Suffix and vector notation, delta and alternating tensor

# Page 5^page=5
Vector vs suffix notation Vector vs su˚x notation Su˚x notation is a local notation. Vector notation is a global notation. For instance ▶ Vector notation: v = (v1, v2, v3) (i.e. the whole vector). ▶ Su˚x notation: vi (i.e. only one component) For a scalar λ ▶ Vector notation: λv = (λv1, λv2, λv3). ▶ Su˚x notation: λvi. 2 23

# Page 6^page=6
Suffix notation Dummy indices and free indices Free indices: Index appearing exactly once in each term that indicates the component of a tensor . ▶ E.g. vi means the i-th component of the vector v. Dummy indices: Indices appearing exactly twice in a term that indicate a sum . ▶ E.g. the dot product a · b = a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3 = 3∑ j=1 aibi can be written in su˚x notation as aibi. 3 23

# Page 7^page=7
Kronecker delta Kronecker delta The Kronecker delta δij is de˝ned by δij = { 1 if i = j, 0 if i ̸= j. Properties. "Substitution tensor": δijaj = ai (i.e. repeated index gets swallowed up) δjiai = aj Dot product in terms of δij: a · b = δijaibj. 4 23

# Page 8^page=8
The Alternating Tensor The Alternating Tensor The Alternating tensor is de˝ned by ϵijk =    0 if any of i, j, k are equal , +1 if (i, j, k) = (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 1) or (3, 1, 2), −1 if (i, j, k) = (1, 3, 2), (2, 1, 3) or (3, 2, 1). It remains unchanged if indices are reordered by a cyclic permutation : ϵijk = ϵjki = ϵkij. the sign changes if any two of the su˚ces are interchanged : ϵijk = −ϵjik. 5 23

# Page 9^page=9
Properties of the Alternating Tensor Properties of the Alternating Tensor The Alternating Tensor can be used to de˝ne the cross product: (a × b)i = ϵijkajbk. is related to the determinant of a matrix: |M | = ϵijkM1iM2jM3k, (row) |M | = ϵijkMi1Mj2Mk3. (column) can be used to de˝ne the scalar triple product: a · (b × c) = ϵijkaibjck. 6 23

Position vector and differential operators Position vector The position vector is r = (x1, x2, x3). We denote its magnitude by r = |r|. Position vector and di˙erential operators We have computed the gradient, divergence and curl of r. ∇r = r r , where r = |r|, ∇ · r = 3, and [∇ × r]i = (0)i, that is, ∇ × r = (0, 0, 0). 10 23

# Page 16^page=16
Coordinate Systems Coordinate Systems Coordinate systems are de˝ned by a set of basis vectors . Vector basis is a set of vectors v1, v2, v3 that are linearly independent: the only scalars λ1, λ2, λ3 satisfying λ1v1 + λ2v2 + λ3v3 = (0, 0, 0) are λ1 = λ2 = λ3 = 0. span the space : Every vector v can be written as a linear combination v = µ1v1 + µ2v2 + µ3v3. 11 23

# Page 17^page=17
Orthogonal and Orthonormal coordinate systems De˝nitions A coordinate system is orthogonal if its basis vectors intersect at 90◦ angles , i.e., vi · vj = 0, for i ̸= j. A coordinate system is orthonormal if it is orthogonal and its basis vectors have magnitude 1 , i.e., ▶ vi · vj = 0, for i ̸= j, and ▶ |vi| = √vi · vi = 1. 12 23

# Page 18^page=18
Usual Cartesian coordinate system Example The usual Cartesian coordinate system ˆi = (1, 0, 0), ˆj = (0, 1, 0), ˆk = (0, 0, 1) is an example of orthonormal coordinate system . 13 23

# Page 19^page=19
Rotating a basis Rotating a basis Let e1, e2, and e3 be basis vectors. If we rotate these basis vectors, we will obtain new basis vectors e′ 1, e′ 2, and e′ 3. This yields a new coordinate system (x′ 1, x′ 2, x′ 3). How do we swtich from one coordinate system to another? 14 23

# Page 20^page=20
Switching between the coordinate systems Switching between the coordinate systems When we say "switch between the coordinate systems (x1, x2, x3) and (x′ 1, x′ 2, x′ 3)" we mean: Let e1, e2, e3 be a basis for the coordinate system (x1, x2, x3). Let e′ 1, e′ 2, e′ 3 be a basis for the coordinate system (x′ 1, x′ 2, x′ 3). By the de˝nition of basis, we can expand any vector v in terms of these bases. That is, v = v1e1 + v2e2 + v3e3, and v = v′ 1e ′ 1 + v′ 2e ′ 2 + v′ 3e ′ 3, for some constants vi and v′ i. How do we get vk's from v′ k's and vice versa? 15 23

# Page 21^page=21
Transformation Matrix Transformation Matrix We have seen that if we de˝ne a matrix L = [Lij] with components Lij = e ′ i · ej, then we have x′ i = Lijxj. This matrix is called the transformation matrix because it allows you to switch between the coordinate systems (x1, x2, x3) and (x′ 1, x′ 2, x′ 3). 16 23

# Page 22^page=22
Properties of the transformation matrix Properties of the transformation matrix The number Lij is simply the cosine of the angle between e′ i and ej. L is orthogonal i.e. LT L = I = LLT . In particular, LijLkj = δik = LjiLjk. Since x′ i = Lijxj and xi = Ljix′ j, we have ∂x′ i ∂xj = Lij and ∂xi ∂x′ j = Lji. 17 23

# Page 23^page=23
Transformation Matrix Example Example Let K be a Cartesian coordinate system with orthonormal basis i1, i2, i3. De˝ne K′ with basis e1 = i1 + i2 + i3, e2 = 2i2, e3 = i1 + 3i2. Let us ˝nd the rotation matrix L = [Lij]. Method 1: i1, i2, i3 is Cartesian, and   e1 e2 e3   =   1 1 1 0 2 0 1 3 0     i1 i2 i3   , thus L =   1 1 1 0 2 0 1 3 0   . 18 23

# Page 24^page=24
Transformation Matrix Example Example Method 2: Using de˝nition. Recall: e1 = i1 + i2 + i3, e2 = 2i2, e3 = i1 + 3i2. L11 = e1 · i1 = 1, L12 = e1 · i2 = 1, L13 = e1 · i3 = 1, L21 = e2 · i1 = 0, L22 = e2 · i2 = 2, L23 = e2 · i3 = 0, L31 = e3 · i1 = 1, L32 = e3 · i2 = 3, L33 = e3 · i3 = 0. 19 23

Tensors in othogonal (Carte- sian) coordinate systems

# Page 26^page=26
Formal definition of a vector Formal de˝nition: transformation rule A vector is a quantity satisfying v′ i = Lijvj. That is, a vector is a quantity which transforms in a certain way under a rotation of coordinates. This is called the transformation rule (of a vector). Transformation (rotation) matrix Lij The matrix Lij has the special property LT = L−1. This allows us to show Lij(Ljk)T = LikLkj = δik. 20 23

# Page 27^page=27
In general Formal de˝nition A quantity is a tensor if each of the free indices satisfy the tranformation rule under rotation of the coordinates. For instance, Rank 2: T ′ ij = LimLjnTmn, Rank 3: T ′ ijk = LimLjnLkpTmnp, Rank 4: T ′ ijkℓ = LimLjnLkpLℓqTmnpq, etc. De˝nition The rank or order of a tensor is the number of free indices. 21 23
